question: As the EU intends to pump EUR 7.4 billion into General Al-Sisi’s regime, it would be interesting to know how many hundreds of millions it has already spent on fortifying the Egyptian border. Can the Commission provide a plausible explanation as to why, despite this assistance, the number of illegal migrants from Egypt and arriving via Egypt from Sudan, Ethiopia and Somalia continues to rise? Also, as with Tunisia, how will the new payments dramatically reverse this trend once and for all?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.7.2024) The Commission works with Member States in a Team Europe approach to deepen comprehensive partnerships with third countries based on mutual interests. Tailor-made partnerships that reflect shared goals can deepen relations and a shared strategic vision.

The EU and Egypt took their cooperation to the level of a Strategic and Comprehensive Partnership, launched with the signature of the Joint Declaration on 17 March 20241, with the aim of deepening their shared stability, peace and prosperity. The partnership covers six key pillars: political relations; economic stability; trade and investment; migration and mobility; security and demography; and human capital.

A financial and investment support package of EUR 7.4 billion for Egypt will underpin the partnership. This package consists of short and longer-term support for macro-economic stabilisation, increased support for investments and targeted support for the implementation of specific strategic priorities.

Disbursements under the macroeconomic stabilisation support (up to EUR 5 billion) are linked to an on-track disbursing International Monetary Fund programme and progress on reforms to be agreed with the Egyptian side. On migration, the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument (NDICI) will support its implementation with EUR 200 million, out of the EUR 7.4 billion, for the period 2024-2027.

In line with the holistic approach to migration laid down in the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum2, EU financial support to Egypt on migration-related programmes will also cover legal migration pathways and mobility schemes, tackling the root causes of irregular migration, combating smuggling of migrants and trafficking in persons, strengthening border management and ensuring dignified and sustainable return and reintegration.

This will complement actions under the European Union Emergency Trust Fund for Africa and reinforce ongoing actions under NDICI. As regards border management, total allocations under NDICI for 2021-2023 amount to EUR 110 million.

The aim is to strengthen the operational capacity of Egypt’s navy and border guards to conduct border surveillance and search and rescue operations at land and sea, including equipment and training. The first equipment delivery took place in the first quarter of 2024. To combat migrant smuggling, the EU is also planning additional support of EUR 20 million.

Along the Central Mediterranean route, departures from Tunisia have decreased by more than 50% so far in 2024, compared to the same period in 2023. Egyptians are the fifth main nationality registered along this route in 2024 so far.
